summary.text: A weather satellite is an Earth observation satellite used mainly to monitor the Earth's weather and climate.
They come mainly in two types: polar orbiting ones that cover the whole Earth, and geostationary ones that hover over one spot on the equator.
Besides tracking storms and clouds, they detect fires, pollution, dust storms and snow cover, and together give nearly continuous global observations.

facts.label: First success
facts.value: TIROS-1, launched by NASA on 1 April 1960

facts.label: Countries flying them
facts.value: US, China, Europe, India, Russia and Japan

facts.label: Newest Meteosat imagers
facts.value: Scan the full Earth disc every ten minutes

items.prompt: A forecaster wants a nonstop view of storms over one stretch of ocean near the equator, all day long. Which kind of satellite fits best?
items.explain: Geostationary satellites hover over the same spot on the equator, so they keep watching one area.

items.prompt: A mission needs to photograph every part of the planet over time, Antarctica and the Arctic included. Which kind of satellite suits it?

options.label: One parked above a single city

items.explain: Polar orbiting satellites cover the entire Earth, while geostationary ones stay over one spot on the equator.

items.prompt: Weather satellites mainly watch storms and clouds. What else can they detect from orbit?
items.explain: Meteorological satellites can also detect city lights, fires, pollution, auroras, dust storms, snow cover and more.

items.prompt: As early as 1946, people were developing the idea of putting weather cameras in orbit. What pushed them?

options.label: A wish to spy on rival navies
Sparse data and costly rocket cameras

items.explain: The idea arose from sparse observation coverage and the expense of using cloud cameras on rockets.

items.prompt: A NOAA satellite launched in 2015 into deep space watches a different kind of weather. What does it watch for?

options.label: Dust storms on the surface of Mars

items.explain: DSCOVR was the first deep space satellite able to observe and predict space weather, detecting solar wind and geomagnetic storms.

items.prompt: Meteosat Third Generation satellites hold steady on three axes instead of spinning like earlier Meteosats. What did that change give designers?

options.label: A much cheaper ride into orbit
No need to carry any fuel at all
A lower and faster path around Earth

items.explain: Being three-axis stabilised rather than spin-stabilised gives greater flexibility in satellite and instrument design.
